questions.stem: A task has a recommended weight limit of 18 kg and an actual load of 27 kg. What is the lifting index?
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: LI = load weight/RWL = 27/18 = 1.5. A value above 1 indicates increased lifting demand relative to the recommended limit.
incorrectOptionExplanations: This reverses the required load-to-limit ratio.
This subtracts the recommended limit from the actual load.
This adds the actual load and recommended limit.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025)
questions.sourceLocation: Yates Chapter 24, NIOSH lifting index, pp. 548-555; NIOSH Revised Lifting Equation

questions.stem: During a lift redesign, the load is moved closer to the worker while all other factors remain unchanged. What is the expected ergonomic effect?
options: The asymmetry multiplier automatically becomes zero
The horizontal multiplier improves and the recommended weight limit increases
The frequency multiplier decreases because the load is closer
The lifting index increases solely because reach is reduced
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: Keeping the load close reduces the moment on the low back, improves the horizontal multiplier, and generally increases the recommended weight limit.
incorrectOptionExplanations: Moving the load closer does not by itself eliminate torso rotation or set the asymmetry multiplier to zero.
Frequency is determined by lift rate and duration, not horizontal location.
Reducing reach generally lowers demand; it does not inherently increase the lifting index.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025)
questions.sourceLocation: Yates Chapter 24, horizontal component and multiplier, pp. 548-551; NIOSH RNLE

questions.stem: A worker uses a pinch grip with high force, wrist deviation, and repeated motion for most of the shift. Which risk-factor combination is most important?
options: Temperature only
Noise and illumination only
Force, awkward posture, and repetition acting together
Age alone
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: Ergonomic risk increases when forceful exertion, awkward posture, and repetition occur together and for sustained durations.
incorrectOptionExplanations: Temperature may matter, but the scenario directly identifies force, posture, and repetition.
Noise and illumination are not the primary exposures described in the task.
Age is an individual characteristic and does not replace task-based exposure analysis.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025)
questions.sourceLocation: Yates Chapter 24, ergonomic definitions and risk factors, pp. 546-548

questions.stem: A safety professional needs a rapid screening tool focused mainly on upper-limb posture during seated microscope work. Which tool is most appropriate?
options: REBA only
NIOSH lifting equation
Fault tree analysis
RULA
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: Rapid Upper Limb Assessment is designed to screen posture, force, and muscle use affecting the neck, trunk, and upper limbs.
incorrectOptionExplanations: REBA evaluates broader whole-body postures and is less specifically focused on upper limbs.
The lifting equation evaluates two-handed manual lifting, not seated upper-extremity posture.
Fault tree analysis evaluates combinations of failures leading to a top event.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025)
questions.sourceLocation: Yates Chapter 24, RULA and REBA, pp. 561-563

questions.stem: A fixed-height assembly bench forces shorter workers to elevate their shoulders and taller workers to bend their trunks. Which redesign is strongest?
options: Provide an adjustable work surface or fixtures that fit the intended user range
Require all workers to use the same posture training
Rotate workers every hour without changing the bench
Select one average worker and design only for that person
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: Adjustability or properly selected fixtures accommodate anthropometric variation and reduce sustained shoulder and trunk loading.
incorrectOptionExplanations: Training cannot overcome a workstation that does not fit the user population.
Rotation may limit duration but leaves the mismatch and exposure in place.
Designing for the average excludes workers at the smaller and larger ends of the population.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025)
questions.sourceLocation: Yates Chapter 24, ergonomic job analysis and workspace design, pp. 546-566

questions.stem: A company rotates employees between two jobs that both require high-force wrist flexion. What is the main weakness of this control?
options: Rotation is always an engineering control
The rotation changes workers but does not meaningfully change the exposure
Rotation eliminates the need to assess force
Rotation guarantees adequate recovery time
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: Effective rotation should alternate different muscle groups or exposure patterns; rotating between similar high-demand tasks provides little recovery.
incorrectOptionExplanations: Job rotation is generally an administrative control, not a physical redesign.
Force remains a key exposure and must still be evaluated.
Recovery depends on the demands of the alternate task and timing; it is not guaranteed.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025)
questions.sourceLocation: Yates Chapter 24, work practice controls and ergonomic job analysis, pp. 546-566

questions.stem: A handheld tool has a narrow hard edge pressing into the palm and transmits high vibration. Which improvement best addresses both exposures?
options: Ask workers to grip the tool more tightly
Add a warning label to the tool body
Redesign the handle with an appropriate grip surface and reduce vibration at the source
Increase production speed to shorten each cycle
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: A better handle distributes pressure while source-level vibration reduction addresses the transmitted mechanical exposure.
incorrectOptionExplanations: A tighter grip increases force and may worsen both contact stress and vibration transmission.
A label communicates risk but does not reduce the physical exposure.
Faster production may increase repetition and does not control tool vibration or edge pressure.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025)
questions.sourceLocation: Yates Chapter 24, ergonomic stressors and work design, pp. 546-566

questions.stem: Which program feature best supports early intervention for work-related musculoskeletal symptoms?
options: Record symptoms only after a lost-time case occurs
Discourage reporting until symptoms become severe
Use discipline when workers request temporary task modification
A nonpunitive reporting process with prompt task evaluation and access to qualified care
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: Early reporting, evaluation, and exposure modification can prevent progression and provide useful information about task design.
incorrectOptionExplanations: Waiting for lost time misses the opportunity to control early, reversible conditions.
Delayed reporting allows exposure and symptoms to progress.
Punitive responses suppress information and undermine prevention.

questions.stem: A reach control must be usable by nearly all operators. Which design principle is generally most appropriate?
options: Design maximum reach for smaller users rather than the average user
Use the 95th-percentile reach for all controls
Use only the mean body dimension
Design reach and clearance using the same percentile direction
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: For reach, a smaller-user percentile helps ensure controls remain accessible; different percentile logic applies to clearance.
incorrectOptionExplanations: A large-user reach value can place controls beyond the reach of smaller users.
The mean excludes substantial portions of the user population.
Reach should generally accommodate smaller users, while clearance often accommodates larger users.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025)
questions.sourceLocation: Yates Chapter 24, ergonomic job design and anthropometric principles, pp. 546-566

questions.stem: Before broadly deploying an industrial exoskeleton, what is the best evaluation approach?
options: Assume reduced muscle activity in one area proves the system is safe
Pilot it with representative tasks and users while measuring benefits, new loads, fit, usability, and unintended risks
Issue one size to all workers and measure only productivity
Replace the task redesign process with exoskeleton training
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: A controlled pilot should evaluate total-system effects, worker variability, transfer of load, compatibility, and operational risks before scale-up.
incorrectOptionExplanations: Reducing one muscle load may shift force or restrict movement elsewhere.
Fit and anthropometric variation are essential, and productivity alone is not a safety evaluation.
Wearable technology should not automatically replace elimination or engineering redesign.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025)
